# Overview

## Background

Attitudes toward immigration vary substantially across individuals and
are shaped by a range of social, economic, and demographic factors.

Education is frequently associated with more positive attitudes toward
immigration, making it a useful focal predictor for examining variation
in immigration attitudes.

This project examines the relationship between education and attitudes
toward immigration in the Netherlands using data from Round 10 of the
European Social Survey (ESS).

## Research Question

**To what extent is education associated with attitudes toward
immigration in the Netherlands?**

The analysis investigates whether respondents with more years of
education tend to report more positive attitudes toward immigration and
whether this association remains after accounting for sociodemographic,
economic, and attitudinal characteristics.

The project demonstrates an end-to-end quantitative analysis workflow in
R, including data cleaning, composite index construction, reliability
analysis, exploratory visualization, multiple linear regression, robust
check, and statistical visualization.

# Analysis

## Data and Variable Construction

The analysis uses ESS Round 10 data and focuses on respondents from the
Netherlands.

Attitudes toward immigration are measured using three survey items
assessing perceptions of immigration's:

1.  economic impact
2.  cultural impact
3.  overall impact on the country

Higher values indicate more positive attitudes toward immigration.

The focal independent variable is years of education. Additional
variables include age, gender, country of birth, perceived household
income, religiosity, household income, cultural values, and social
trust.

### Import Data

The raw ESS dataset is not included in this repository.

```{r import-data}
ESS10 <- read_csv("ESS10.csv")
```

### Select Netherlands Sample

```{r select-data}
ess_nl <- ESS10 %>%
  filter(cntry == "NL") %>%
  select(
    age = agea,
    gender = gndr,
    born_country = brncntr,
    education = eduyrs,
    household_income = hinctnta,
    religiosity = rlgdgr,
    immigration_economic = imbgeco,
    immigration_cultural = imueclt,
    immigration_country = imwbcnt,
    social_trust = ppltrst,
    cultural_value = imptrad,
    perceived_income = hincfel
  )
```

### Data Cleaning

Special ESS response codes representing responses such as *Don't know*,
*Refusal*, and *No answer* are recoded as missing values.

```{r clean-data}
ess_nl_clean <- ess_nl %>%
  mutate(
    age = na_if(age, 999),

    gender = if_else(
      gender %in% c(7, 8, 9),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(gender)
    ),

    born_country = if_else(
      born_country %in% c(7, 8, 9),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(born_country)
    ),

    education = if_else(
      education %in% c(77, 88, 99),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(education)
    ),

    household_income = if_else(
      household_income %in% c(77, 88, 99),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(household_income)
    ),

    religiosity = if_else(
      religiosity %in% c(77, 88, 99),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(religiosity)
    ),

    immigration_economic = if_else(
      immigration_economic %in% c(77, 88, 99),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(immigration_economic)
    ),

    immigration_cultural = if_else(
      immigration_cultural %in% c(77, 88, 99),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(immigration_cultural)
    ),

    immigration_country = if_else(
      immigration_country %in% c(77, 88, 99),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(immigration_country)
    ),

    social_trust = if_else(
      social_trust %in% c(77, 88, 99),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(social_trust)
    ),

    cultural_value = if_else(
      cultural_value %in% c(7, 8, 9),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(cultural_value)
    ),

    perceived_income = if_else(
      perceived_income %in% c(7, 8, 9),
      NA_real_,
      as.numeric(perceived_income)
    )
  )
```

### Construct Immigration Attitude Index

```{r construct-index}
analysis_data <- ess_nl_clean %>%
  mutate(
    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),

    born_country = factor(
      born_country,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c(
        "Born in Netherlands",
        "Born outside Netherlands"
      )
    ),

    immigration_attitude = rowMeans(
      across(
        c(
          immigration_economic,
          immigration_cultural,
          immigration_country
        )
      ),
      na.rm = FALSE
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    education <= 21 | is.na(education)
  )
```

### Reliability

Cronbach's alpha is used to assess the internal consistency of the three
immigration-attitude items.

```{r reliability}
attitude_items <- analysis_data %>%
  select(
    immigration_economic,
    immigration_cultural,
    immigration_country
  )

alpha_result <- psych::alpha(attitude_items)

alpha_result$total$raw_alpha
```

The three items show acceptable internal consistency (**Cronbach's α ≈
0.78**) and are therefore combined into a composite index.

## Exploratory Analysis

Because years of education are recorded as integer values, jittering is
used to reduce overplotting.

```{r focal-relationship}
p_relationship <- ggplot(
  analysis_data,
  aes(
    x = education,
    y = immigration_attitude
  )
) +
  geom_jitter(
    width = 0.18,
    height = 0.08,
    alpha = 0.18,
    size = 1.6,
    colour = "#526D82"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    colour = "#C45A45",
    fill = "#E9B4A7",
    linewidth = 1.2,
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 21, 3)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 0:10,
    limits = c(0, 10)
  ) +
  labs(
    title =
      "Education Is Positively Associated With Immigration Attitudes",
    x = "Years of education",
    y = "Immigration attitude index",
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p_relationship
```

The exploratory relationship is positive: respondents with more years of
education tend to report more favorable attitudes toward immigration.

## Regression Analysis

To ensure that coefficient changes across model specifications are not
driven by changes in sample composition, all regression models are
estimated using the same complete-case sample.

```{r regression-sample}
model_data <- analysis_data %>%
  drop_na(
    immigration_attitude,
    education,
    age,
    gender,
    born_country,
    perceived_income,
    religiosity,
    household_income,
    cultural_value,
    social_trust
  )

nrow(model_data)
```

Three regression specifications are estimated:

-   **Model 1** estimates the bivariate association between education
    and immigration attitudes.
-   **Model 2** introduces sociodemographic controls.
-   **Model 3** adds economic and attitudinal predictors, including
    social trust and cultural values.

```{r regression-models}
model_1 <- lm(
  immigration_attitude ~ education,
  data = model_data
)

model_2 <- lm(
  immigration_attitude ~
    education +
    age +
    gender +
    born_country +
    perceived_income +
    religiosity,
  data = model_data
)

model_3 <- lm(
  immigration_attitude ~
    education +
    age +
    gender +
    born_country +
    perceived_income +
    religiosity +
    household_income +
    cultural_value +
    social_trust,
  data = model_data
)
```

### Model Comparison

```{r model-comparison}
gof_map <- data.frame(
  raw = c(
    "nobs",
    "r.squared",
    "adj.r.squared"
  ),
  clean = c(
    "N",
    "R²",
    "Adjusted R²"
  ),
  fmt = c(
    0,
    3,
    3
  )
)

modelsummary(
  list(
    "Bivariate" = model_1,
    "Controls" = model_2,
    "Extended" = model_3
  ),
  stars = TRUE,
  statistic = "({std.error})",
  gof_map = gof_map,
)
```

Because all three models use the same respondents, changes in the
education coefficient across specifications reflect changes in model
specification rather than changes in sample composition.

Education remains positively associated with immigration attitudes after
the introduction of sociodemographic, economic, and attitudinal
characteristics.

## Coefficient Plot

The coefficient plot summarizes the estimated relationships in the
extended model and displays 95% confidence intervals.

```{r coefficient-data}
coefficient_data <- broom::tidy(
  model_3,
  conf.int = TRUE
) %>%
  dplyr::filter(
    term != "(Intercept)"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    term_label = dplyr::case_when(
      term == "education" ~
        "Education",

      term == "age" ~
        "Age",

      term == "genderFemale" ~
        "Female",

      term ==
        "born_countryBorn outside Netherlands" ~
        "Born outside Netherlands",

      term == "perceived_income" ~
        "Perceived income difficulty",

      term == "religiosity" ~
        "Religiosity",

      term == "household_income" ~
        "Household income",

      term == "cultural_value" ~
        "Cultural value",

      term == "social_trust" ~
        "Social trust",

      TRUE ~ term
    ),

    significant = if_else(
      p.value < 0.05,
      "Significant",
      "Not significant"
    )
  )
```

```{r coefficient-plot}
p_coefficients <- ggplot(
  coefficient_data,
  aes(
    x = reorder(term_label, estimate),
    y = estimate
  )
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey55"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = conf.low,
      ymax = conf.high
    ),
    width = 0.12,
    linewidth = 0.8,
    colour = "grey45"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      shape = significant
    ),
    size = 3,
    colour = "#2F5D50"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title =
      "Key Predictors of Immigration Attitudes",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Estimated coefficient",
    shape = NULL,
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

p_coefficients
```

# Model Evaluation

## Robust Standard Errors

HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are calculated for the
extended model.

```{r robust-se}
robust_results <- lmtest::coeftest(
  model_3,
  vcov = sandwich::vcovHC(
    model_3,
    type = "HC3"
  )
)

robust_results
```

The substantive conclusions remain unchanged when HC3 robust standard
errors are used.

## Multicollinearity

```{r multicollinearity}
vif_results <- car::vif(model_3)

vif_results
```

VIF values are low, indicating no meaningful multicollinearity among the
predictors.

# Key Findings

-   Higher levels of education are consistently associated with more
    positive attitudes toward immigration across the regression
    specifications.

-   The association remains statistically significant after accounting
    for sociodemographic, economic, and attitudinal characteristics.

-   Social trust and cultural values are also positively associated with
    immigration attitudes in the extended model.

-   The main conclusions remain substantively unchanged when HC3 robust
    standard errors are used.

-   VIF values indicate no meaningful multicollinearity among
    predictors.

Because all regression specifications use the same complete-case sample,
changes across models are not driven by differences in sample
composition.

The models explain a modest proportion of variation in immigration
attitudes, which is reasonable for an individual-level social attitude
outcome influenced by many social and contextual factors.

Because the analysis uses **cross-sectional observational survey data**,
the results should be interpreted as statistical associations rather
than causal effects.
